The useful discipline is keeping snapshots small enough that a diff is actually readable — which usually means asserting on a projection of the output rather than all of it.

title: The test suite you don't trust costs the same and tells you nothing
excerpt: At a 2% flake rate over 400 tests, a third of runs fail for reasons unrelated to the change. The suite has stopped being a signal and become a toll.
opening:
There's a threshold where a test suite crosses from asset to liability, and it's reached faster than people expect because the maths is multiplicative.

Once the team's default interpretation of a red build is "probably flaky, re-run it", every genuine failure is also interpreted that way. The suite is now actively harmful: it costs full price and provides no information.

title: Cognitive load is the constraint, not headcount
excerpt: A team owning four services in one domain is fine. The same team owning four services across four domains is overloaded regardless of how many people it has.
opening:
Capacity planning counts people and work. It rarely counts how much a team must hold in mind to make a safe change, which is what actually limits throughput.

The symptom isn't missed deadlines. It's caution — changes get smaller and slower because nobody is confident about the blast radius, and that shows up as low velocity with no obvious cause.

title: Root cause: human error, action item: be careful
excerpt: A review that identifies an action as the cause and adds a process step has learned nothing. The question is why the system permitted that action to have that consequence.
opening:
Blameless postmortems are widely claimed and less widely practised. The tell is an action item about attention, training, or an added approval step.

Someone ran a command against production. The useful questions are why that was possible from where they were standing, why it wasn't obvious which environment they were in, and why it took eleven minutes for anyone to notice.

title: Your hiring process selects for recent interview practice
excerpt: Algorithmic puzzles measure a real skill that correlates weakly with the job. Work samples predict better and cost more to run, which is the point.
opening:
A cheap process that selects poorly is more expensive than an expensive process that selects well. The bill just arrives eighteen months later, disguised as a performance management problem.

Work-sample tasks resembling actual work require someone to design them and read the results carefully. That's the cost, and it's small relative to a single mis-hire on a team of six.

title: Code review is for shared understanding
excerpt: It catches some defects, less reliably than tests. Its durable value is a second person who knows why the change was made — and that reframes what a good review is.
opening:
If review's purpose is defect detection, then thorough is better and delay is justified. If its purpose is knowledge distribution, a comment that improves the code slightly while delaying the merge by a day is a poor trade.

The second framing is closer to reality, and it makes questions more valuable than corrections. A question that reveals the author and reviewer disagree about how the system works is worth a week of nitpicks.

title: Estimates without conditions are noise
excerpt: "Three weeks" and "three weeks unless the API lacks bulk updates, in which case six" are different statements. The second lets someone de-risk today.
opening:
A single-number estimate discards the only genuinely useful information it contains: what the estimator is uncertain about.

That's also why estimates get treated as commitments — they're delivered as though there's no uncertainty, so the listener reasonably assumes there isn't. Attaching the conditions changes what the conversation is about, from a date to a set of unknowns someone can go and resolve.

title: A senior IC track that exists on the careers page
excerpt: A credible individual-contributor ladder needs real architectural scope, roadmap influence, and comparable compensation. Without those, the title fools nobody.
opening:
Organisations that lose good engineers to management often have a technical ladder on paper. What they don't have is a senior IC whose architectural decisions actually stick, or whose compensation matches the equivalent manager.

Engineers evaluate the track by looking at who's on it and what happened to them, which is a much better signal than the job architecture document.

title: On-call is a design constraint on the system
excerpt: A rotation that wakes someone twice a week isn't a staffing problem to solve with more people. It's the system telling you something about its failure modes.
opening:
The usual response to painful on-call is to spread the pain — larger rotation, follow-the-sun coverage, better compensation for the disruption.

Those help and they treat the symptom. Page volume is a measurable property of the architecture, and a rotation nobody dreads is achievable, but only by treating each recurring page as a defect rather than as the cost of running software.

title: Documenting decisions, not architecture
excerpt: The successor can read the code. What they can't recover is which constraints were real, which were preferences, and what was rejected.
opening:
Architecture documentation describes what exists, which is the part that's discoverable by reading the system. It goes stale immediately and duplicates something authoritative.

A short record of each significant decision — options considered, constraint that decided it, what would change the answer — doesn't go stale, because it's a record of a moment. It's also the thing every new person actually asks about.

title: Meetings are a synchronisation primitive
excerpt: Treating them as a scheduling problem misses the point. The question is what state needs to be consistent across how many people, and how stale it can be.
opening:
Calendar complaints usually produce calendar solutions: fewer meetings, shorter meetings, meeting-free days. Those help and they don't address why the meeting existed.

Thinking about it as synchronisation makes the alternatives visible. Some information needs everyone consistent immediately; most tolerates lag and belongs in writing, where it's also durable and searchable.

title: The reorg that moved boundaries without moving ownership
excerpt: Teams were restructured around the new domain map and the services stayed where they were. Every change now crosses two teams that no longer talk.
opening:
Reorganisations redraw reporting lines faster than they redraw system ownership, and for a period — often a long one — the two don't match.

During that period, the coordination cost of every change goes up, and it's attributed to the usual suspects: unclear priorities, technical debt, communication problems. The actual cause is a mismatch between who owns the code and who owns the outcome.

title: Your second measurement is where the surprises are
excerpt: The first one confirms your hypothesis, because you chose what to measure based on the hypothesis. A different tool at a different layer disagrees.
opening:
Profiling has a confirmation problem built into its workflow. You suspect a component, you instrument that component, and you find it consuming time — which it is, along with everything else.

The measurement that changes your mind is usually at a different layer: wall-clock on the request path rather than CPU in the function, or the same workload at a different time of day.

title: What a flame graph doesn't show you
excerpt: It shows where CPU time went, not time spent blocked — which on most web workloads is the majority. It also averages away the occasional catastrophe.
opening:
Flame graphs are the default profiling artefact and they answer one specific question well. The failure is using them for questions they can't answer.

Blocked time doesn't appear. Tail behaviour is aggregated into a shape optimised for totals, so a function that's fine 99% of the time and terrible otherwise looks unremarkable. Both of those are frequently the actual problem.

title: Divide the latency budget before you defend it
excerpt: 200ms for an endpoint means nothing until it's split across the steps. With a split, a regression is attributable; without one, you have a debate.
opening:
Writing the budget down is itself the valuable part. Teams routinely discover a step consuming a third of the total that nobody had thought of as a cost — serialisation, an auth lookup, a logging call that does more than it looks like.

Afterwards, a regression names itself: the database step went from 80ms to 140ms and everything else held.

title: The mean is nobody's experience
excerpt: 120ms average is compatible with 95% at 50ms and 5% at 1.5 seconds. A page making twenty requests hits p99 more often than not.
opening:
Averages are the default aggregation in most dashboards and they describe no actual user. Worse, they're stable — a growing tail barely moves the mean, so the dashboard looks fine while the experience degrades for a specific group.

The compounding point is the one that changes minds: with twenty requests per page load, hitting the 99th percentile at least once is more likely than not.

title: Every cache is a staleness decision
excerpt: Time-based expiry is simple and serves stale data for the TTL. Event-based invalidation is correct and couples every writer to every cache.
opening:
Adding a cache is a few lines of code and a permanent commitment to reasoning about correctness. The commitment is what people underestimate, because the initial version is obviously beneficial and obviously correct.

It stops being obviously correct the first time someone writes to the database through a path that doesn't know the cache exists — a migration, an admin tool, another service.

title: Fixing an N+1 so it stays fixed
excerpt: The batch loader solves today's instance. A query-count assertion in a test solves the one someone reintroduces in six weeks with a new field.
opening:
N+1 regressions recur because the conditions that produce them recur: someone adds a field to a response and resolves it per-row, which is the natural way to write it.

The fix that lasts isn't in the resolver, it's in the test suite. Without an assertion, the second instance surfaces the same way as the first — as a latency graph, three deploys after the cause.

title: Measuring on the hardware your users have
excerpt: Development machines are unrepresentative in a consistent direction. A CPU throttle in the profiler is a cheap approximation of the median device.
opening:
Every performance measurement taken on a developer laptop is optimistic, and it's optimistic by a factor that varies with the workload — which means you can't apply a correction.

Throttling the CPU during profiling isn't a substitute for testing on real hardware, and it costs nothing and catches the worst of it before code review.

title: The optimisation that made things slower
excerpt: A cache added in front of a fast query added a network hop, a serialisation step, and an invalidation bug — for a lookup that was already using an index.
opening:
Optimisations get applied by pattern rather than by measurement: caching is good, so cache. The cost of the cache — the hop, the serialisation, the memory, the invalidation logic — is rarely compared against the cost of the operation it replaces.

For an indexed primary key lookup on a warm database, that comparison frequently comes out against the cache.

title: Load tests that don't resemble load
excerpt: A hundred threads hitting one endpoint with identical parameters exercises your cache. Real traffic has a distribution, and the distribution is the test.
opening:
Synthetic load tests are usually written for convenience: one endpoint, fixed parameters, maximum concurrency. They produce a number and the number is meaningless because everything after the first request is served from cache.

Replaying a sample of real request logs is more work to set up and it's the only version that tells you anything about capacity.

title: Perceived performance and the spinner you didn't need
excerpt: An optimistic update makes a 300ms operation feel instant. A spinner makes the same operation feel like waiting, and the measured latency is identical.
opening:
Some of the largest available wins aren't in the code path at all. The same 300ms feels instantaneous when the interface responds immediately and reconciles afterwards, and feels slow when it displays a loading state.

The engineering cost is a rollback path for the optimistic case. That's real work, and it's frequently less than the work required to get the operation from 300ms to 100ms.

title: Time your quickstart with a stopwatch
excerpt: If it takes twenty minutes to a working call, it isn't a quickstart regardless of the heading. The success criterion is narrow and measurable.
opening:
The quickstart is the only page most readers will ever open, and its job is one thing: produce a request that returns real data as fast as possible.

Everything else — the configuration reference, the architectural context, the full auth model — competes with that job. A page that explains concepts before producing a result loses a fraction of its readers at every paragraph, and they don't come back.

title: Every code sample is an untested assertion
excerpt: It was true when written and nothing keeps it true. Extracting fenced blocks and typechecking them turns drift into a build failure.
opening:
Documentation code samples are the highest-trust content on the site and the least verified. A renamed export or a changed signature invalidates them silently, and the reader who hits it concludes the product is unreliable — which, in the specific sense that its documentation lies, it is.

The fix is mechanical: extract the fences, compile them against the current workspace, fail CI on error.

title: Reference should be generated, explanation should be written
excerpt: One is mechanical and drifts. The other encodes judgement and doesn't. Merging them produces a document that fails both readers.
opening:
The most common documentation structure interleaves "what this function accepts" with "why you'd use it", and serves neither reader well. Someone doing a lookup wades through prose; someone trying to understand gets a parameter table.

Separating them also clarifies what to automate. Reference material should never be typed by a human, and explanation should never be generated.

title: Your support volume maps to error text
excerpt: Support tickets correlate far more tightly with unhelpful error messages than with documentation gaps, and almost nobody checks the correlation.
opening:
Documentation teams look at page analytics to decide what to write. The higher-signal dataset is usually sitting in the support system: the exact strings people paste when they open a ticket.

Those strings are your error messages. Fixing the top ten — what happened, what was expected, where, what to do — reliably removes more support load than any new page.

title: Write down what the product doesn't do
excerpt: An explicit limits page prevents a whole category of conversation that starts "I assumed". It also forces the team to know its own limits.
opening:
Documentation describes capability. What costs users the most time is discovering boundaries — the undocumented limit, the combination that isn't supported, the thing that works until it's under load.

Stating them plainly reads as confidence rather than weakness, and writing the page is frequently the first time anyone has enumerated them internally.

title: Your search log is a table of contents you didn't write
excerpt: The queries returning nothing are a prioritised list of missing pages, composed by the people who needed them.
opening:
When readers can't find things, the usual responses are a better search box or more pages. Neither addresses a structure organised around how the team thinks about the product rather than how users arrive at it.

Users arrive with a task. The zero-result queries in the search log are that mismatch, itemised, and they're usually sitting unexamined in an analytics tool nobody has opened.

title: Docs review belongs in the pull request
excerpt: Documentation written after the release describes what shipped from memory. Written alongside, it's reviewed by someone who knows whether it's true.
opening:
The separate documentation ticket, filed at the end of a project, is where accuracy goes. By the time anyone picks it up, the details are reconstructed and the person who knew them has moved on.

Requiring the doc change in the same pull request is unpopular and it's the only workflow I've seen where the documentation and the behaviour describe the same system.

title: Changelogs written for the person upgrading
excerpt: A list of merged pull request titles is a git log with extra steps. What's needed is what breaks, what to do about it, and what's now possible.
opening:
Auto-generated changelogs are complete and useless. They report every change at the same weight, in the author's language, with no indication of whether a reader needs to act.

The reader has one question — does this upgrade require anything from me — and answering it requires a human to sort changes into breaking, notable, and everything else.

title: Screenshots are a maintenance liability
excerpt: They go stale invisibly and at scale. Either generate them from the running product or design pages that don't depend on them.
opening:
A screenshot is accurate on the day it's taken and there's no mechanism to detect when it stops being. Users notice — an interface that doesn't match the picture undermines confidence in everything else on the page.

Generating them in CI from the real application is genuinely achievable and rarely done. The alternative is being deliberate about how few you need.

title: Documentation for the reader who arrived from Google
excerpt: Most readers land on an interior page with no context. A page assuming they read the introduction is a page that fails most of its audience.
opening:
Documentation is written in order and read at random. The typical arrival is a search result pointing at a page three levels deep, with no exposure to the concepts introduced earlier.

Which means each page needs enough orientation to stand alone — what this is, what it assumes, where to go next — without duplicating the whole guide on every page.

title: Spend your novelty budget where it differentiates
excerpt: Every unfamiliar technology consumes part of a small, finite budget for things that can surprise you. On a team of three that budget is very small.
opening:
The question about a new database isn't whether it's better. It's whether it's better by enough to justify being the team that has never operated it, at 2am, with no colleague who has seen this failure before.

Sometimes the answer is yes, and it should be yes for the thing that makes your product different. Everywhere else, the dullest available option is the correct one.

title: Buy the boring parts
excerpt: Advice written for large organisations assumes a platform team. Without one, every piece of infrastructure competes directly with product work.
opening:
Managed services look expensive on the invoice and the comparison is usually made against zero rather than against the real alternative, which is a founder debugging certificate renewal on a Saturday.

That cost doesn't appear on any statement, and on a team of three it's the largest cost you have. The premium is generally worth paying well past the point where the spreadsheet says otherwise.

title: Ship the ugly version to the three people who asked
excerpt: A feature nobody has used is a hypothesis. Polishing before validation spends the scarce resource on the part that might be wrong.
opening:
The instinct is to make it good before showing anyone, and on a small team that instinct is expensive — engineering time is the entire budget.

The smallest version that answers the question, given to the customers who requested it, closes the loop in days. The gap between what people request and what they use is routinely large, and it's only observable after shipping something.

title: Half a page per decision beats a wiki nobody wrote
excerpt: Comprehensive documentation won't get written on a small team. A short decision log — chosen, rejected, why — will, and it's what a successor actually needs.
opening:
Every system on a small team has exactly one person who understands it. That's arithmetic rather than a process failure, and the mitigation has to be proportionate to the time available.

The successor can read the implementation. What they can't recover is which constraints were real and which were preferences, and that fits in a paragraph written while it's fresh.

title: Generalists until the system won't fit in one head
excerpt: Specialisation is efficient at scale and costly below it, because every handoff between specialists is a queue longer than the work.
opening:
Engineers who touch the database, the API, the frontend and the deploy pipeline make worse decisions in each area and much better decisions about the whole. Below a certain size that trade is strongly favourable.

The transition point is when a single person can no longer hold the system in their head — and it arrives considerably later than most teams assume it does.

title: Say no on the record
excerpt: Small teams die of dilution more than of any single wrong decision. A visible list of what was declined turns awkward individual conversations into one position.
opening:
Each individual commitment is reasonable. The aggregate is a team maintaining eleven things and advancing none, and there's no single decision you could point at as the mistake.

Writing refusals down — what, when, why — makes the position durable and revisitable. Without the record, every declined request gets relitigated from memory, individually, forever.

title: The monolith is fine
excerpt: Service boundaries solve organisational scaling problems. Adopting them at four engineers imports the operational cost without the problem they address.
opening:
Splitting services is a response to teams stepping on each other — independent deploys, independent ownership, independent scaling. Those are real benefits available to organisations that have the problem.

At four engineers there is no coordination problem to solve, and what you've bought instead is network calls where function calls were, distributed transactions, and a tracing requirement.

title: Automate the third time, not the first
excerpt: The first occurrence is a task. The second is a coincidence. The third is a pattern, and by then you know enough about its shape to automate it correctly.
opening:
Premature automation is a specific small-team failure: a script that encodes a process you didn't understand yet, which then has to be maintained and worked around.

Waiting until the third occurrence costs two manual repetitions and buys a much better understanding of which parts are stable and which vary. The tooling that results is smaller and survives longer.

title: One environment that matters
excerpt: Staging, QA, preview and production is four things to keep in sync with two engineers. Preview environments per branch plus production is usually enough.
opening:
Environment proliferation is inherited from larger organisations where each one serves a distinct team's needs. On a small team they mostly serve as places for configuration to drift.

Ephemeral per-branch environments that are created and destroyed with the pull request give you the isolation without the maintenance, because nothing persists long enough to diverge.

title: Support as a product research channel
excerpt: On a small team the engineers can answer tickets directly. The information density is far higher than any survey and the loop closes in an afternoon.
opening:
Routing support away from engineers is standard practice and it's a scaling adaptation, not a default. Before you need it, having engineers in the queue is one of the strongest advantages a small team has.

The person who can fix the confusing error message is reading the ticket about it, and the fix ships the same day.

title: State the question before building the prototype
excerpt: A prototype built to impress gets polished. One built to answer a question gets thrown away once it's answered, which is the point.
opening:
Without a stated question, a prototype becomes a foundation by accident and its shortcuts become architecture. That's the most common way throwaway code becomes permanent.

Writing the question first — will users understand this, is the API fast enough, does this model support the reports finance needs — determines both what to build and, more usefully, what not to.

title: Instrument before you ship, or don't ask about launch
excerpt: Analytics added afterwards can't answer questions about the launch period, which is the only time you observe genuinely first-time use.
opening:
Instrumentation gets scheduled after the feature because the feature is the deliverable. The consequence is that the most informative two weeks in a feature's life pass unobserved.

There's a second benefit to doing it first, and it's the one that improves the product: if you can't express success as a number before building, the specification is vaguer than it looked.

title: Feature flags need an owner and an expiry
excerpt: Each flag doubles the number of states. The combination nobody tested is where the bug is, and a two-year-old flag is dead code nobody dares remove.
opening:
A flag is a temporary branch that persists because removing it requires proving nothing depends on it, and nobody wants to be the person who was wrong about that.

The mechanism that works is external: a scheduled report of flags past their removal date, addressed to a named owner. Intention doesn't clean them up; a recurring nag does.

title: Fake doors and concierge versions
excerpt: Measuring click-through on something that doesn't exist, or serving the first ten customers by hand, both cost days. A quarter of engineering costs a quarter.
opening:
A disproportionate share of engineering goes into features almost nobody uses, and this is knowable in advance more often than teams admit.

The techniques feel like not-building, which is why they get skipped. They're also the difference between validating demand for a few days of effort and validating it for a few months of it.

title: Percentage rollouts give you a control group for free
excerpt: A launch to everyone has one chance to be right and no comparison. Rolling out by percentage makes the problem small and the metric interpretable.
opening:
The rollback argument for progressive delivery is well understood. The measurement argument gets less attention and is at least as valuable.

Without a cohort that didn't get the feature, you can't tell whether the metric moved because of your change or because it was a Tuesday in a month with a holiday. The comparison is the only thing that makes the number mean anything.

title: You can't deprecate what you can't measure
excerpt: Without per-customer usage data, removal is either postponed indefinitely out of caution or executed blind and breaks someone important.
opening:
Deprecation stalls on a question nobody can answer: who is still using this. In the absence of data, the safe-feeling choice is to leave it, and the accumulated weight of things nobody dares remove becomes its own tax.

The blocker is instrumentation rather than policy, and it's usually a day of work to add usage counters keyed by account.

title: The roadmap item that was a support workaround
excerpt: A feature request repeated by five customers may be five people describing the same underlying obstacle in the vocabulary of their current workaround.
opening:
Requests arrive as solutions. "We need bulk export" is a proposal, and behind it there's a task the person is trying to complete, which may have a much smaller answer.

The discipline is asking what they do with the export. Frequently it turns out that four of the five would be better served by something you could build in a week, and the fifth genuinely needs the export.

title: Shipping the removal
excerpt: Taking a feature away is a product change deserving the same care as adding one: notice period, migration path, and a way to tell who's affected.
opening:
Removals get treated as cleanup and executed with far less rigour than additions, despite having a much higher chance of making someone's day worse.

The asymmetry is worth naming: adding a feature nobody wants costs you engineering time. Removing one someone depends on costs them their workflow, and they didn't get a say.

title: Defaults are the product
excerpt: The overwhelming majority of users never open settings. Every option you add is a decision you've declined to make on their behalf.
opening:
Adding a setting feels accommodating and it's frequently an abdication — the team couldn't agree, so both behaviours ship and the user arbitrates.

The cost isn't only the user's. Every option multiplies the states you support, test and document, and the combinations are where the bugs are. A well-chosen default serves more people than a well-built preference.

title: Measuring the thing rather than its proxy
excerpt: Sessions, clicks and time-on-page are proxies for value, and optimising a proxy hard enough eventually detaches it from the thing it stood for.
opening:
Proxy metrics are chosen because the real outcome is hard to measure, then they become targets, then they become the definition of success.

The detachment is gradual and usually invisible until someone notices that engagement is up and retention is flat. Keeping a harder-to-measure outcome metric alongside the proxy is the cheapest defence available.

title: Triage is the job now
excerpt: Writing the library was the fun part and it's finished. What determines whether the project survives is whether issues get a response.
opening:
The transition catches maintainers by surprise. The creative work is largely done within the first year, and what remains is a sustained obligation with no end date and no schedule.

Templates and labels help with throughput. They don't address the actual cost, which is that every open issue is an implied promise, and the count only moves in one direction.

title: Is a bug fix a breaking change?
excerpt: Strictly, if anyone depends on the buggy behaviour, yes. Practically, treating every fix as major makes the version number meaningless.
opening:
Semantic versioning is precise about categories and silent about judgement, and the judgement is where every real argument happens.

The workable position is to document the intent — what's covered by the compatibility promise, what's explicitly not — so the calls are at least predictable. Undocumented behaviour isn't part of the contract, but only if you said so before someone relied on it.

title: Audit your dependency tree by maintainer count
excerpt: The risk isn't primarily malicious packages. It's abandonment — one maintainer who stops, and an advisory arriving eighteen months later with no upstream fix.
opening:
Dependency risk is usually discussed in terms of supply-chain attacks, which are real and rare. The failure that actually happens is quieter.

Sorting the tree by last release date and number of maintainers takes an afternoon and identifies a small number of genuinely fragile links — usually packages nobody chose directly, pulled in three levels down.

title: `>=2.1.0` is a floating pin
excerpt: A constraint written to satisfy a security advisory permits every future major version, including the one that removes the API you use.
opening:
The build breaks on a day nobody changed anything, which is the most expensive kind of break because the cause isn't in the diff and the first hour goes to looking for it there.

Unbounded ranges get introduced with good intentions — a minimum version to clear an advisory — and they're pins that float upward without limit. Lockfiles protect you and not your published package's consumers.

title: A project with one maintainer has already failed
excerpt: The failure just hasn't been observed. Burnout is silent — responses get slower, then stop, and there's no announcement.
opening:
The single-maintainer package is a structural risk to everyone depending on it and to the maintainer, who has an obligation with no relief valve.

What helps is structural rather than motivational: a second person with publish rights, a documented release procedure, and a written scope so that out-of-scope requests can be declined once rather than negotiated repeatedly.

title: The reporter who took the time to make a reproduction
excerpt: The best contributions to a library aren't features. They're precisely described edge cases from production, and the reporting experience determines whether you get them.
opening:
A good bug report is expensive to produce. Someone hit a problem, reduced it to a minimal case, and wrote it up — that's an hour of unpaid work donated to your project.

The experience they get determines whether they do it again. The ones who get a fast acknowledgement come back with the next one; the ones who don't patch it privately, and you never learn the class of bug exists.

title: Publishing trust is per-package and easy to orphan
excerpt: Renaming a package or a workflow file breaks the trust relationship silently. The next release fails at publish, after the tag is cut.
opening:
Keyless publishing through CI is a substantial security improvement and it introduces a configuration binding that's invisible in the repository.

The trust is registered against a specific package name and a specific workflow path. Change either — a rename, a refactor of the CI directory — and the relationship no longer matches. Nothing warns you until a release is halfway done.

title: What ships in the tarball
excerpt: Packaging strips some files by convention, includes others by accident, and the result is only observable by installing the published artefact.
opening:
The gap between the repository and the published package is a recurring source of bugs that are invisible in development and total for consumers — a missing directory, a stripped configuration file, a dependency needed at runtime but declared as a dev dependency.

Installing the packed artefact into a scratch project, in CI, is the only check that reflects what users get.

title: Undeclared dependencies that npm hoisting hid
excerpt: A package imported without being declared resolves fine under a flat node_modules and fails immediately under a strict one. Half your users hit it.
opening:
Hoisting makes undeclared dependencies work by accident, which means the bug is invisible to anyone using the tooling that hoists — frequently including the entire team that maintains the package.

Under strict resolution the import fails outright. The report arrives from a user whose setup differs from yours, and the first instinct is to assume their environment is broken.

title: Scope, written down, declines requests for you
excerpt: Without a stated scope, every out-of-bounds feature request is an individual negotiation. With one, it's a link and a sentence.
opening:
Maintainer time goes to explanation more than to code, and much of that explanation is repeating the same boundary in different words to different people.

A short document stating what the project is for, and what it deliberately doesn't do, converts a recurring negotiation into a reference. It also makes the project easier to evaluate, which is worth something on its own.

title: Measure retrieval separately from generation
excerpt: An end-to-end evaluation hides which half is failing, and the fixes for each are entirely different. Most quality problems are retrieval problems.
opening:
Attention goes to the model because that's the part that feels like the system. In most retrieval-augmented applications, output quality is determined by whether the right documents were fetched — a search problem with decades of prior work behind it.

Evaluating the pipeline as a single unit gives you one number that goes up and down for reasons you can't attribute.

title: Your evaluation set is leaking
excerpt: Examples curated by the person who tuned the prompts, or sampled from a period whose distribution has shifted, produce a number that won't survive production.
opening:
Leakage in evaluation sets is usually indirect rather than blatant. Nobody trained on the test set; someone assembled it while building the system, from the same data, with the same intuitions about what a representative example looks like.

A set collected from real traffic at a different time, labelled by someone who didn't build the system, will report a worse number. That's the point of it.

title: Define the fallback before the model is slow
excerpt: A feature with no specified behaviour when the model times out has specified it implicitly, as an error page.
opening:
Model calls are network requests to a system with variable and occasionally very long latency. Designing around the median produces a p99 that fails, and the failure path is whatever the framework does by default.

Streaming, a strict deadline, and a degraded-but-useful fallback are the three mechanisms. The fallback is the one that gets deferred, and it's the one users experience.

title: Prompts are code with no test suite
excerpt: A prompt edit is a behaviour change deployed with no type check, no test, and often no review — and it directly determines output.
opening:
Of everything in a model-backed system, the prompt has the most influence over behaviour and the least process around changing it. It's frequently edited in a config file by whoever noticed a bad output.

Versioning prompts as artefacts with an eval run attached brings them roughly up to the standard of the rest of the codebase, which is a low bar they currently don't clear.

title: Keep a regression set of things that used to break
excerpt: Improvements on one dimension routinely regress another, and without a fixed set of previously-bad inputs there's no way to see it happen.
opening:
Prompt and retrieval changes are evaluated against whether they fix the problem that prompted them. What they break is discovered later, by users, in an area nobody was looking at.

A growing collection of inputs that previously produced bad output, run on every change, is the cheapest available guard. It takes minutes to add an entry and it accumulates value indefinitely.

title: Chunking is where retrieval quality is won
excerpt: Splitting on a fixed token count severs the context a passage needs to be interpretable. The embedding is then of a fragment that means nothing on its own.
opening:
Chunk size gets tuned as a hyperparameter and treated as an implementation detail. It determines what the embedding actually represents, which makes it one of the most consequential decisions in the pipeline.

A passage split mid-argument, or separated from the heading that gives it meaning, produces a vector for text that no longer says anything. No amount of model quality recovers that.

title: Hybrid search beats pure vector more often than not
excerpt: Semantic similarity misses exact identifiers, error codes and product names — which is a large share of what people actually search for.
opening:
Vector search handles paraphrase and conceptual similarity well, and it's notably weak at the thing keyword search is trivially good at: finding the document containing this exact string.

Users search for error codes, SKUs and function names. A hybrid ranking that combines both signals is more work than either alone and consistently outperforms both.

title: Deletion has to be as reliable as ingestion
excerpt: A document removed at the source and still present in the index is a correctness problem and frequently a compliance one.
opening:
Ingestion gets built carefully because it's the visible path. Deletion is added later, often as a best-effort cleanup, and it fails quietly.

The result is an index that accumulates content the source has removed — including, eventually, something someone had a legal right to have deleted. That's a different category of problem from stale search results.

title: Budget the majority of the timeline for data plumbing
excerpt: Extraction, deduplication, format normalisation, permission handling and keeping an index in sync are the work. That's not a planning failure.
opening:
The expectation going in is model work. The reality is that the model is an API call and everything around it is a data engineering project with a search component.

Teams that plan for this ship on schedule. Teams that treat it as overhead discover it as slippage, and describe the project afterwards as having been harder than expected.

title: A hundred of your own examples beats any leaderboard
excerpt: Published benchmarks measure someone else's task on someone else's distribution, often with contamination nobody has ruled out.
opening:
Benchmarks are useful for excluding options and close to useless for choosing among the top few, where the differences are within the noise of your specific workload.

A small evaluation set drawn from your own traffic — a hundred examples, labelled carefully — can be built in a day and predicts production behaviour far better than any public ranking.
